Imagine all possible policies (derived from their parent philosophies) on a topic as belonging to a set of N functions written such that outcomes are expressed along P number of metrics in m variables (same variables in every scenario; it's the same world/nation), where the function Ni expresses the behavior of the "pure" form of the philosophy along the ith metric as extrapolated from the nearest real world examples (empirical curve-fitting; build the model up one variable at a time).

Laissez-Faire Capitalism (functions Li)

Lopportunity(capital access, taxation, education, social security, ... , m)
Lequality(capital access, taxation, education, social security, ... , m)

Socialism (functions Si)

Sequality(capital access, taxation, education, social security, ... , m)
Swealth(capital access, taxation, education, social security, ... , m)
...
SP(capital access, taxation, education, social security, ... , m)

...

N-ism (functions Ni)

Nopportunity(capital access, taxation, education, social security, ... , m)
Nequality(capital access, taxation, education, social security, ... , m)
Nwealth(capital access, taxation, education, social security, ... , m)
...
NP(capital access, taxation, education, social security, ... , m)

Now imagine you would like to propose a policy with an objective of, say, maximize opportunity. You would find that this occurs once, twice, perhaps an unknown o times in each of the N philosophies (it's actually quite difficult to imagine a m-variable/dimension space, lol). For simplicity, say it only occurs once in each philosophy.

We find how to create maximum opportunity by taking the partial derivative of Nopportunity with respect to each of the m variables. Now we have as many choices for each of the m variables as we have political philosophies; i.e.:

"The level of taxation required in Laissez-Faire Capitalism to create maximum opportunity is _____"
"The level of taxation required in Socialism to create maximum opportunity is _____"
"The level of taxation required in N-ism to create maximum opportunity is _____"

And so on for each of the m variables. Our assumption of a single extremum also means that there is also a "locked-in" value for each of the other m variables within a philosophy as well. This particular combination of variables produces values of the other performance metrics that (most likely) are not extrema.

"Because we are using _____ level of taxation, _____ degree of capital access, ..., and _____ amount of m, this means that while opportunity is maximized in N-ism, equality, wealth, ..., P are set at these (P-1) values _____, _____, ..., _____."

Can you see how you would simple back-iterate to the "best" policy choice now?

"Oh, well I don't like now N-ism leaves us with low levels of equality if we choose our variables that way."

"Well, go and see what N-ism's variables for maximum equality are."
